newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-ELS BEATS ELKINGTON IN REGIONAL FINAL OF ANDERSEN MATCHPLAY.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ELS BEATS ELKINGTON IN REGIONAL FINAL OF ANDERSEN MATCHPLAY.

text.p: U.S. Open champion Ernie Els of South Africa beat Australian Steve Elkington 2-up in a regional final of the match-play Andersen Consulting World Championship of Golf Tuesday to advance to a semifinal against a familiar rival, Colin Montgomerie of Britain.

Els had a 3-hole lead on the River Course at Blackwolf Run with three to play, but did not close out the match until Elkington hit his approach shot into the water to the left of the green on the 469-yard, par-four 18th hole.
With his victory in the international region, Els joined three other regional champions in the Andersen Consulting world finals, set for next January 3-4 in Scottsdale, Arizona.
Montgomerie (Europe), Davis Love (U.S.) and Hajime Meshiai (Japan) had qualified previously. The overall champion will collect $1 million from the total purse of $3.75 million.

Els is rapidly compiling one of the best match-play records of the 1990s. The lanky 27-year-old has won an unprecedented three consecutive Toyota World Match Play titles and has a 3-1-1 record in the Presidents Cup.
Montgomerie, his scheduled semifinal opponent in Scottsdale, has twice been Els's foil in the U.S. Open -- both times in near match-play situations.
Els beat Montgomerie and Loren Roberts in a playoff in the 1994 Open, then outgunned Montgomerie and Tom Lehman down the stretch at Congressional Country Club last month.
Els also beat Montgomerie in the final of the 1994 World Match Play. "I don't know what it is," he said. "I just like match play."
Earlier Tuesday, Els beat Nick Price of Zimbabwe, 3 and 2, and Elkington beat fellow Australian and Andersen defending champion Greg Norman, 2 and 1, in the regional semifinals.
Then against Elkington, Els won the 12th and 13th holes with birdies to go 3-up, and the players halved the next two holes.
Elkington went to the 16th tee dormie, but the match was just heating up. Els pulled his second shot into the water on the 560-yard par-five and Elkington made a birdie to get one hole back.
On the 168-yard 17th, Elkington made another birdie after hitting his 8-iron to within four feet.
Suddenly, Elkington was 1-down with one hole to play. "His tail was up going to the 18th," Els said. "I could see that. Then he hit a brilliant drive right down the middle."
Els also placed his ball in the fairway on the 18th, forcing Elkington to gamble.
"I've got to make birdie, because I figure Ernie is going to make par from where he is," Elkington said. "I had to go at the flag."

Elkington slightly pulled his 3-iron from 212 yards, and the ball splash-landed in a temporary water hazard to the left of the green. When he hit another ball into the water -- he needed to hole out for par from the fairway to have any chance -- the match was over.

Els had survived, but it was nothing like the scare he got flying in here when his chartered plane tried to land at Sheboygan County Airport on Sunday afternoon. "We were coming down, and another plane was approaching us," Els said.
"We had to go up quite rapidly. It was scary. I never thought those things still happened, but I guess they do. We made it, anyway."
